lessons.title: The Road Back to the Throne: Restoration of the Monarchy 1660

before.content_html:
In May 1660, Charles II sailed from the Netherlands and entered London to cheering crowds. Eleven years earlier his father had been executed by Parliament; now the monarchy, the House of Lords and the Church of England were being rebuilt at speed. The Restoration was not, however, a simple winding back of the clock. Parliament emerged from the settlement stronger than before, and the religious and political tensions that had caused the Civil War were postponed rather than solved.

Why the Republic Collapsed

Oliver Cromwell, Lord Protector since 1653, died on 3 September 1658. His son Richard Cromwell took over but had no military reputation and no support from the army. Within nine months Richard had resigned and the Protectorate had collapsed. England drifted through a succession of rival regimes: the recalled Rump Parliament, the army Council of Officers, and brief military governments. Trade suffered, taxes rose and ordinary people grew tired of rule by soldiers.

Key Fact

Cromwell died in September 1658. Within sixteen months his Protectorate had collapsed, the army was split, and General Monck was marching south from Scotland to call free elections.

General Monck and the Convention Parliament

General George Monck commanded the army in Scotland. In January 1660 he marched south to London with disciplined troops and demanded that the old ‘Long Parliament’ be properly dissolved and free elections called. The result was the Convention Parliament, which met in April 1660. It was not summoned by a king and so technically had no legal authority — but it had popular support, royalist sympathies and a clear mandate to negotiate the king’s return.

The Declaration of Breda

From his exile in the Dutch town of Breda, Charles II issued a careful public statement in April 1660, drafted with his minister Edward Hyde. The Declaration of Breda made four key promises designed to win over moderate opinion.

First, a free pardon for all who had fought against the Crown — except those Parliament chose to punish. Second, ‘liberty to tender consciences’ in religion, leaving the detail to Parliament. Third, payment of the army’s arrears so the soldiers would not block the king’s return. Fourth, a settlement of disputed land titles to be agreed by Parliament. Crucially, every difficult question was passed to Parliament — meaning Charles returned by invitation, not by conquest.

Parliament accepted the Declaration on 1 May 1660. Charles entered London on his thirtieth birthday, 29 May 1660, with bells ringing and wine running in fountains. Samuel Pepys, watching from the Strand, recorded that the streets were ‘strewed with flowers’ and the bonfires went on all night.

The Act of Indemnity and Oblivion

In August 1660 the Convention passed the Act of Indemnity and Oblivion. Most former Parliamentarians were pardoned and the past was officially forgotten. The exception was the regicides — the men who had signed Charles I’s death warrant in 1649. Ten were hanged, drawn and quartered at Charing Cross. The bodies of Cromwell, his son-in-law Henry Ireton and the judge John Bradshaw were dug up from Westminster Abbey, hanged at Tyburn and beheaded. Cromwell’s skull was displayed on a pike on Westminster Hall for over twenty years.

What Was Actually Restored?

The settlement restored three things: the monarchy itself, the House of Lords (abolished in 1649) and the Church of England with its bishops. Bonfires, maypoles and Christmas were once again legal. But several powerful Crown weapons did not come back. The Court of Star Chamber and other prerogative courts stayed abolished. Feudal tenures, which had given the king income from his major landowners, were gone for good. In their place the king was given a fixed yearly income voted by Parliament — the first time the Crown had to live on a parliamentary allowance.

Key Fact

The Restoration brought back the monarchy, the House of Lords and the Church of England. It did NOT restore Star Chamber, the prerogative courts or feudal Crown income — meaning the new king depended on Parliament for money.

A common student misconception is that 1660 healed the country. It did not. The two issues that had caused the Civil War — who controlled religion, and who controlled the king’s money — were left unresolved. Parliament was now stronger because it controlled royal finance, but the king still claimed the right to choose his ministers and direct foreign policy. Twenty-eight years later these same tensions, sharpened by the question of a Catholic heir, would bring down Charles II’s brother James II in the Glorious Revolution of 1688.

For now, in the summer of 1660, the country celebrated. Soldiers were paid off and sent home. Royalist gentry began returning to their estates. Charles II rewarded the men who had brought him back: Monck became Duke of Albemarle, Hyde became Earl of Clarendon and Lord Chancellor. The hard arguments about how the new monarchy would actually be financed and what to do about Dissenters had been postponed — and the next Parliament, the Cavalier Parliament of 1661, would take a much harder line than the Convention had done.

Build chains: identify an effect (e.g. the Crown lost its old feudal income), then explain why this mattered (the king now needed parliamentary grants), then link to a wider consequence (Parliament gained leverage over royal policy for the rest of the reign). practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of the Declaration of Breda on the return of Charles II in 1660.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• The Declaration won over moderate opinion by promising a pardon for most Parliamentarians, which made it safer for former Roundheads to accept the king's return rather than fight to keep him out.
• By offering 'liberty to tender consciences', it reassured Dissenters that they would not face immediate persecution — though Parliament later overturned this with the Clarendon Code.
• The promise to pay the army's arrears removed the most dangerous obstacle: a hostile army of around 40,000 men. General Monck was able to disband most of the New Model Army peacefully.
• By referring every difficult issue (religion, land, indemnity) back to Parliament, it established that Charles returned by parliamentary invitation, not by conquest — strengthening Parliament's long-term position.
• The carefully limited promises also meant that the new king kept his options open on patronage and ministers, allowing him to reward supporters such as Monck and Hyde.
[8 marks — Mastering: at least two developed effects with precise causal chains; Secure: two effects with clear explanation; Developing: more than one effect but limited explanation; Emerging: simple description of the Declaration with little focus on effects.]

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Convention Parliament of 1660.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• It was not summoned by a king. The Long Parliament had been dissolved and the Convention met in April 1660 on General Monck's authority — making it technically illegal until Charles II later confirmed its acts.
• It was elected with a clear royalist majority. Many MPs had previously sat under Charles I and the new House of Commons accepted the Declaration of Breda within days of meeting.
• It passed the Act of Indemnity and Oblivion in August 1660, pardoning most Civil War actions but excluding the regicides.
• It voted Charles II a fixed yearly income of around £1.2 million from customs and excise — an amount that proved far too small in practice.
[4 marks — 2 marks per feature: 1 for identification, 2 for a developed supporting detail. Two features must be clearly separated.]

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of General Monck's march south in 1660.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time, Monck's disciplined army was the only force capable of imposing order on the rival army factions in London. Without him, England might have collapsed into a third Civil War.
• He insisted on free elections rather than a continuation of the purged Long Parliament — this was the decisive step that allowed a royalist majority to be returned.
• He provided cover for Charles II's negotiations with Edward Hyde at Breda, signalling to royalists that the army would not block a Restoration.
• Over time, his actions established the principle that a peaceful return of the monarchy was possible — a precedent later echoed in 1688 when William of Orange's army backed another constitutional settlement.
• His personal reward (Duke of Albemarle, Master of the Horse) showed how Charles II used patronage to bind former Parliamentarian generals into the new regime.
[8 marks — Mastering: importance both at the time AND over time, with sustained explanation; Secure: clear importance at the time with some longer-term link; Developing: importance at the time only; Emerging: brief description of Monck's actions.]

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which the situation in England was similar before and after the Restoration of 1660.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Two Ways Similar or Different
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Parliament continued to control taxation. Under both the Commonwealth and the Restoration settlement, the Crown could not raise major new taxes without parliamentary consent — customs duties and the hearth tax were voted by Parliament.
• Religious tension remained unresolved. Both before and after 1660, England contained large numbers of Dissenters (Presbyterians, Independents, Quakers, Baptists) who could not accept the official church.
• The army was still a key political question. Cromwell's New Model Army had been politically powerful; after 1660 the question of who controlled the small standing army would remain a flashpoint.
[4 marks — 2 marks per way: 1 for identification, 2 for development. Two ways must be clearly separated.]

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of the Act of Indemnity and Oblivion on English society in the years after 1660.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• It allowed most former Parliamentarians and New Model Army soldiers to return to civilian life without fear of arrest — important for stability, since this group included thousands of men with military experience.
• By excluding the regicides, it satisfied royalist demands for revenge without provoking a wider purge. Ten were executed; others fled to the Netherlands or New England.
• The exhumation and hanging of Cromwell, Ireton and Bradshaw was a public statement that the Republic had been a crime — the displayed skull on Westminster Hall acted as a permanent visual warning.
• Over time the Act made it harder for old Civil War grievances to be raised in court, helping to bury the conflict at a legal level even though religious and political tensions persisted.
• It also created a class of dispossessed regicide families and exiled radicals, some of whom would surface again in plots such as the Rye House Plot of 1683.
[8 marks — Mastering: at least two developed effects with explicit causal links; Secure: two effects with clear explanation; Developing: more than one effect but limited development; Emerging: descriptive narrative of the Act.]

practice_questions.text: 'The Restoration of 1660 changed the relationship between Crown and Parliament more than it preserved it.' Discuss the role of Parliament, finance and religion in the Restoration settlement.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments that the Restoration changed the relationship:
• The Crown lost its prerogative courts (Star Chamber abolished 1641, not restored) and feudal income, meaning the king depended on parliamentary grants for the first time.
• Charles II returned by parliamentary invitation, not by conquest — establishing the principle that Parliament could create as well as serve a monarch.
• Parliament increasingly used finance as leverage: the chronic gap between the king's income and his needs forced repeated negotiations.

Arguments that the Restoration preserved continuity:
• The monarchy, House of Lords and Church of England were all restored, with bishops and the Book of Common Prayer back in place.
• The king kept the right to choose ministers, direct foreign policy and command the (small) army.
• In law, all acts of the Republic were declared void — the legal fiction was that the reign of Charles II began in 1649, denying any constitutional break.

Judgement guidance:
• Strong answers will weigh both sides and reach a substantiated conclusion — for example, that the change in royal finance was the single most consequential shift, because it set the agenda for the conflicts of the rest of the reign.
• Use precise terminology: indemnity, prerogative, customs, hearth tax, Anglican, Dissenters.
[16 marks + 4 SPaG — Mastering: substantiated overall judgement, both sides developed, precise terminology; Secure: clear argument with both sides covered; Developing: one side developed more than the other; Emerging: descriptive with limited argument.]

lessons.title: The Cavalier Parliament and the Religious Settlement

before.content_html:
A New Parliament, an Older Mood

The Convention Parliament that brought Charles II home was relatively moderate. The Parliament that followed was not. Elections in spring 1661 returned the Cavalier Parliament — overwhelmingly young, royalist and Anglican. Many MPs had lost lands or relatives in the Civil War. They were determined to punish the religious groups they blamed for the regicide and to lock the Church of England’s privileges back into law. The result was a chain of statutes, passed between 1661 and 1665, that historians call the Clarendon Code.

The Four Laws of the Clarendon Code

The Clarendon Code was a misleading name from the start. Edward Hyde, Earl of Clarendon, was Lord Chancellor while the laws were passed, but he personally favoured wider toleration and tried to soften the bills. The pressure for harsh measures came from the Cavalier Parliament itself, not from Clarendon.

The Corporation Act of 1661 required all officers of borough corporations to take Anglican communion and reject the Solemn League and Covenant — effectively purging Presbyterians from local government. The Act of Uniformity of 1662 forced every clergyman to use the Book of Common Prayer and to accept Anglican ordination. The Conventicle Act of 1664 made it illegal for more than five people outside one household to meet for non-Anglican worship. The Five Mile Act of 1665 banned ejected ministers from coming within five miles of any town or any place where they had previously preached.

The Great Ejection of 1662

The Act of Uniformity gave clergy until 24 August 1662 — St Bartholomew’s Day — to conform. Around 2,000 ministers refused and were ejected from their parishes. This Great Ejection created at a stroke a permanent body of Protestant Dissenters — men with congregations and no churches. Some emigrated to America. Most stayed and preached in private houses, barns and woods, despite the laws.

Key Fact

The Cavalier Parliament passed four laws between 1661 and 1665: Corporation Act 1661, Act of Uniformity 1662, Conventicle Act 1664 and Five Mile Act 1665. Together they restored Anglican monopoly and ejected around 2,000 ministers in the Great Ejection of 24 August 1662.

Who Were the Dissenters?

The Code targeted four main groups. Presbyterians wanted a national Calvinist Church without bishops. Independents (or Congregationalists) believed each congregation should govern itself. Baptists insisted on adult baptism. Quakers, founded by George Fox, refused oaths, would not remove their hats to magistrates and were jailed in their thousands — including the writer John Bunyan, imprisoned in Bedford gaol from 1660 to 1672 where he wrote ‘The Pilgrim’s Progress’. The collective name for all these groups was Nonconformists or Dissenters; together they probably numbered around five per cent of the English population.

Charles II versus His Parliament

Charles personally preferred toleration — partly to ease the position of his fellow Catholics, partly out of practical sympathy for those who had supported the Restoration. In March 1672 he issued the Declaration of Indulgence, suspending the penal laws against Dissenters and Catholics by royal prerogative. The Cavalier Parliament refused to vote war taxes for the Third Dutch War unless he withdrew it. Charles backed down in March 1673; Parliament then passed the First Test Act, requiring all officeholders to take Anglican communion. The episode showed that Parliament, not the Crown, controlled the religious settlement.

The Convention had voted Charles a yearly income of around £1.2 million from customs, excise and the new hearth tax (a charge on every fireplace, introduced 1662). The figure proved far too small — perhaps two-thirds of what was actually needed. Every time Charles wanted extra money for war or court, he had to ask Parliament. That gave MPs constant leverage over royal policy, especially religious policy. The 1672–73 Indulgence collapse is the clearest example: Parliament traded supply for the withdrawal of toleration.

Key Fact

The 1672 Declaration of Indulgence suspended the penal laws against Dissenters and Catholics. The Cavalier Parliament forced Charles to withdraw it in March 1673 by withholding war taxes, then passed the First Test Act requiring all officeholders to take Anglican communion.

By the mid-1670s the religious settlement looked solid on paper. In practice, Dissenters worshipped quietly in private; magistrates enforced the laws unevenly; and Charles had learned that he could not buy religious peace without parliamentary consent. The pattern was already set: a hard line in statute, softer enforcement on the ground, and constant friction between Westminster and Whitehall whenever the king tried to widen toleration. The grievances created by the Code — especially the exclusion of Presbyterians from public life and the imprisonment of Quakers in their thousands — would resurface during the Exclusion Crisis of 1679–81 and again in the Toleration Act after the Glorious Revolution of 1688. The most lasting effect was institutional: a permanent body of English Protestant Dissenters who would later build their own academies, found their own congregations and shape political opposition for generations.
before.exam_tip_html: For a ‘4 marks — Describe Two Features’ question on the Clarendon Code, choose two clearly separate statutes (e.g. the Act of Uniformity 1662 and the Five Mile Act 1665) and give each a developed supporting detail. Markers want two features clearly separated, not one paragraph blurring them together. Avoid the common error of crediting Edward Hyde with writing the Code — the Cavalier Parliament drove it through against his preference for toleration.

• The Act of Uniformity of 1662 required every clergyman to use the Book of Common Prayer and accept Anglican ordination, with a deadline of St Bartholomew’s Day, 24 August 1662.
• The Conventicle Act of 1664 made it illegal for more than five people outside one household to meet for non-Anglican worship, targeting Dissenter congregations.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Great Ejection of 1662.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Around 2,000 Puritan and Presbyterian ministers were expelled from the Church of England for refusing to use the Book of Common Prayer.
• It took effect on 24 August 1662, St Bartholomew’s Day, the deadline set by the Act of Uniformity for clergy to conform.
• It created a permanent body of Protestant Dissenters — preachers without legal pulpits — who continued to gather in private houses and barns.

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of the Act of Uniformity 1662 on religious life in England.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• It produced the Great Ejection of around 2,000 ministers in August 1662, removing experienced preachers from parish life and leaving many congregations without their familiar clergy.
• It created a permanent class of Dissenters — Presbyterians, Independents, Baptists, Quakers — who continued to meet illegally and were targeted by the Conventicle and Five Mile Acts.
• It re-established the Book of Common Prayer as the only legal liturgy, locking Anglican worship into the parish system across the country.
• Over time it pushed Nonconformist groups into private worship, family-based education and emigration to the American colonies, shaping religious patterns long after the reign.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the 1672 Declaration of Indulgence for relations between Crown and Parliament.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time, the Declaration suspended the penal laws against Dissenters and Catholics by royal prerogative, attempting to bypass the Cavalier Parliament’s religious settlement.
• It triggered a confrontation in 1672–73: Parliament refused to vote war taxes for the Third Dutch War unless Charles withdrew the Declaration, which he did in March 1673.
• Parliament then forced through the First Test Act, requiring all officeholders to take Anglican communion — this drove James, Duke of York and Lord Treasurer Clifford from office.
• Significance over time: it set a pattern in which Parliament used finance to control religious policy, a precedent that would shape the Exclusion Crisis and the Glorious Revolution settlement of 1689.

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of the Conventicle and Five Mile Acts on Dissenters.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• The Conventicle Act 1664 made it illegal for more than five people outside one household to meet for non-Anglican worship, criminalising the ordinary gatherings of Quakers, Baptists and Independents.
• The Five Mile Act 1665 banned ejected ministers from coming within five miles of any town or place where they had previously preached, cutting them off from their old congregations.
• Together the Acts pushed Dissenter worship into private houses, woods and clandestine meetings, while filling local gaols with Quakers in particular.
• John Bunyan was held in Bedford gaol from 1660 to 1672 for unlicensed preaching, where he wrote ‘The Pilgrim’s Progress’ — a long-term cultural effect of the persecution.

Mastering: Multiple effects developed with named individuals and causal chains.

practice_questions.text: Argue, using the religious settlement of 1660–1673, that Parliament rather than the Crown controlled religious policy in Restoration England. Discuss the role of the Cavalier Parliament, the Crown’s preferences and royal finance.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
• The Cavalier Parliament drove the Clarendon Code through despite Edward Hyde’s and Charles II’s preference for wider toleration, showing MPs set the boundaries of permitted worship.
• Parliament forced Charles to withdraw the 1672 Declaration of Indulgence in March 1673 by withholding war taxes, then passed the First Test Act of 1673.
• Royal finance gave Parliament permanent leverage: the £1.2 million annual grant was always too small, so Charles needed parliamentary supply for any war or major project.

Arguments to weigh against:
• Charles II retained the formal right to issue royal proclamations and could attempt to suspend penal laws — the 1672 Indulgence shows he could act, even if he had to retreat.
• In day-to-day enforcement, magistrates and bishops applied the Code unevenly: persecution of Dissenters varied locally as much as nationally.
• The king’s personal preference shaped the climate — Charles disliked persecuting his own brother for Catholicism and used patronage to protect favoured Dissenters.

A strong response weighs constitutional power, finance and royal prerogative and reaches a substantiated overall judgement.

Mastering: Substantiated overall judgement, both sides developed, precise terminology.
Secure: Clear argument with both sides covered.
Developing: One side developed more than the other.
Emerging: Descriptive with limited argument.
[16 marks + 4 SPaG]

lessons.title: The Cabal, Party Politics and Rule Without Parliament

before.content_html:
The Fall of Clarendon

Edward Hyde, Earl of Clarendon, had been Charles II’s chief minister since 1660. He survived the religious settlement, the marriage to Catherine of Braganza in 1662 and the sale of Dunkirk to France — but he could not survive the disaster of the Second Dutch War. The Dutch raid on the Medway in June 1667, when Admiral De Ruyter towed the English flagship out of Chatham, made Clarendon a public scapegoat. Parliament impeached him; Charles dismissed him; and Clarendon fled to France in November 1667, dying in exile in 1674. With Clarendon gone, the king turned to a new style of government: not a single chief minister, but a small inner circle of five.

The Cabal Ministry, 1668–1674

The Cabal took its nickname from the initials of its five members — Clifford, Arlington, Buckingham, Ashley and Lauderdale — though the word ‘cabal’ meaning a secret faction was already in use. They were not a unified team. They disagreed on religion, on France and on the Dutch. What held them together was the king’s confidence and shared work on his most secret project: the Treaty of Dover.

Sir Thomas Clifford was a Catholic convert and Lord Treasurer 1672–73, who pushed the Stop of the Exchequer in January 1672 to keep the Crown solvent. Henry Bennet, Earl of Arlington, ran foreign policy and patronage as Secretary of State. The Duke of Buckingham was Charles’s childhood friend, a witty courtier and a religious sceptic. Anthony Ashley Cooper (later Earl of Shaftesbury) was a former Cromwellian who supported toleration and would soon switch sides. The Duke of Lauderdale ran Scotland with a free hand for the king. They worked separately rather than as a cabinet, and Charles deliberately kept them divided so that no one of them could dominate.

The Secret Treaty of Dover, 1670

In May 1670 Charles signed the Treaty of Dover with Louis XIV of France. Two of the Cabal — Clifford and Arlington — knew the full text, including the secret clause in which Charles promised to declare himself a Catholic at a suitable moment in return for French troops and a subsidy. The other three Cabal ministers were shown only a sham public version, in which Charles agreed to join France in war against the Dutch. The Crown received an initial £225,000 from Louis. The arrangement bound English foreign policy to France for the rest of the reign and made Charles personally beholden to Louis XIV.

Key Fact

The Cabal of 1668–1674 was Clifford, Arlington, Buckingham, Ashley and Lauderdale — whose initials spelled the nickname. They negotiated the secret 1670 Treaty of Dover with Louis XIV, binding England to France for the rest of the reign in return for a subsidy.

The Test Act and the Break-Up of the Cabal

When Charles issued the Declaration of Indulgence in 1672, he expected Parliament to vote the taxes for the Third Dutch War. Parliament refused unless he withdrew it. He withdrew it in March 1673; Parliament passed the First Test Act. The consequences were political. Clifford, by now openly Catholic, resigned the Treasurership and died within months. James, Duke of York, the king’s heir, refused to take the Anglican test and resigned as Lord High Admiral — the first public confirmation that he was Catholic. Shaftesbury fell out with the king over Catholic toleration in 1673 and was dismissed in November. Buckingham was forced out in 1674 by impeachment. By the end of 1674 the Cabal was finished.

From Faction to Party

After the Cabal, Charles relied on the Earl of Danby (Lord Treasurer 1673–79) to manage Parliament with patronage and pensions. Danby tried to build a stable Anglican royalist majority — the beginning of what historians call the Court party. Against him, Shaftesbury organised an opposition of those alarmed by France, by secret Catholic plans and by Crown corruption — the Country party. The labels Whig and Tory only emerged during the Exclusion Crisis of 1679–81, but the underlying division was already in place. England was developing real party politics for the first time.

The Personal Rule, 1681–1685

After the dissolution of the Oxford Parliament on 28 March 1681, Charles refused to summon another. He governed for the last four years of his reign through a small council, the Treasury commission, and his own household. He could afford to do this for two reasons. First, customs and excise revenue grew strongly through the 1680s as English trade boomed. Second, Louis XIV paid Charles a fresh subsidy of around £385,000 between 1681 and 1685 in return for English neutrality. The combination kept the Crown solvent without parliamentary supply.

The personal rule was politically successful in its own terms. The discovery of the Rye House Plot in 1683 allowed Charles to purge Whig sympathisers from corporations using legal challenges to their borough charters. By 1685 around fifty corporations had surrendered their charters and accepted new ones written in the Crown’s favour. James II, when he succeeded in February 1685, inherited a Parliament of Tory loyalists and a Treasury that had run a small surplus in the previous year — the strongest royal position in fifty years.

Key Fact

Charles II ruled without Parliament from March 1681 until his death in February 1685. He paid for it through booming customs and excise revenue and a French subsidy of around £385,000 from Louis XIV in return for English neutrality.

lessons.title: Charles II: The King and His Court

before.content_html:
A King Shaped by Exile

Charles II was thirty when he returned to England in 1660. He had spent eleven years in exile, much of it short of money, in France, the Spanish Netherlands and the Dutch Republic. The experience left him pragmatic, charming, distrustful and determined never to go ‘on his travels’ again. Contemporaries described him as tall, dark, witty and easy in conversation; the diarist John Evelyn admired his manners but worried about his morals. Behind the charm was a politically realistic king who valued discreet management over open confrontation.

The Court at Whitehall

The English court in 1660 was not a palace but a sprawling complex of around 2,000 rooms beside the Thames at Whitehall. Whitehall Palace mixed government offices, private royal apartments, kitchens, chapels and lodgings for around a thousand permanent staff and hangers-on. Public rooms were open to anyone gentlemanly enough to look the part; private rooms were guarded. Access to the king moved by stages, from the public rooms to the bedchamber, where only a handful of courtiers were admitted. Reaching the bedchamber was the surest sign of political favour.

Key Fact

Whitehall Palace had around 2,000 rooms and roughly 1,000 staff. Charles II’s court was organised by access — from public chambers to the private bedchamber. Reaching the inner rooms meant political favour; being kept in the outer rooms meant exclusion.

Catherine of Braganza

In May 1662 Charles married Catherine of Braganza, a Portuguese Catholic princess. Her dowry was extraordinary: £360,000 in cash, the cities of Bombay and Tangier, and trading rights in Brazil and the East Indies. The marriage was politically successful as a Portuguese alliance against Spain. It was personally a sadness. Catherine miscarried at least three times and never produced a living heir; the lack of a Protestant heir was the seed of the Exclusion Crisis fifteen years later. Catherine endured Charles’s public mistresses with quiet dignity and lived in England until her widowhood, returning to Portugal in 1693.

Royal Mistresses as Political Actors

Charles had at least seven acknowledged royal mistresses, and fathered at least fourteen illegitimate children. They were not private matters — they were court appointments. Barbara Villiers, Countess of Castlemaine, dominated the court 1660–70 and was rumoured to influence appointments. Nell Gwyn, an actress from Drury Lane, became his most popular mistress, born poor and politically harmless — her crude wit pleased crowds. Louise de Kéroualle, Duchess of Portsmouth, arrived from France in 1670 with the encouragement of Louis XIV; she remained close to Charles for fifteen years and was widely (and rightly) seen as a French diplomatic asset. Court mistresses were not signs of frivolity but channels of patronage: who got near them got jobs, contracts and titles.

It is tempting to picture the Restoration court as a long carefree party after Puritan austerity. The reality was darker. Theatre and print were censored under the Licensing Act of 1662 and Sir Roger L’Estrange ran the Surveyor of the Press from 1663. Many courtiers were quietly Catholic, in a country where Catholicism was illegal. Mistresses had French diplomatic links. Below the wit, the same religious and political tensions that had caused the Civil War were unresolved. Tim Harris and other modern historians have argued the ‘merry monarch’ label hides a politically skilful king navigating real party formation.

Court Fashions and the Vest

Charles brought back French and Spanish fashions from his exile. Long curled wigs replaced the Puritan crop. Heeled shoes, lace, and slashed sleeves marked status. In October 1666, in the middle of the Plague-and-Fire crisis, Charles personally introduced the vest — a long sleeveless garment worn under a coat — as a deliberately English alternative to the French doublet. The diarist Samuel Pepys recorded the king’s announcement and bought one within days. The vest is the ancestor of the modern waistcoat. Beyond clothing, the court favoured Italian opera, French formal dance, racing at Newmarket and tennis. Charles had a real-tennis court built at Whitehall and was often beaten by the better players.

The Court as a Political Machine

Court life mattered politically because it was the engine of patronage. Offices in the royal household, pensions, peerages and military commissions were all distributed through the court. The Earl of Danby, Lord Treasurer 1673–79, used systematic court patronage to manage Parliament — estimates suggest he had perhaps 200 MPs receiving Crown money in some form. Court mistresses negotiated for their kin. Foreign ambassadors lobbied through their countrymen. The court was therefore not separate from politics but the inner stage on which politics happened.

Charles II was the most physically active king England had seen in a century. He had a real-tennis court built at Whitehall and another at Hampton Court; Pepys recorded watching him play on early mornings. He swam in the Thames at Battersea, walked at speed through St James’s Park (a long-running joke at court was that no minister could keep up), and rode at his Newmarket racing stables, which he visited twice a year for the spring and autumn meets. Sociable habits had political uses: a courtier who walked with the king for an hour got a hearing that no formal audience could match. Even leisure was a route to access.

Key Fact

Charles II’s court at Whitehall was the engine of patronage. Mistresses such as Barbara Villiers, Nell Gwyn and Louise de Kéroualle were not private matters but channels of access — Louise de Kéroualle in particular was openly a French diplomatic asset arriving with Louis XIV’s encouragement.
before.exam_tip_html: For an ‘Explain Significance’ question on Charles II’s court, structure your answer in two halves. Significance at the time: how the court functioned as the centre of patronage and access (the bedchamber, the mistresses, Danby’s parliamentary management). Significance over time: how French fashions and the vest shaped English style, how court Catholicism fed the fears of the Popish Plot, how the failure to produce a Protestant heir set up the Exclusion Crisis. Markers reward both timescales explicitly.

before.content_html:
Outbreak in St Giles, Spring 1665

In April 1665 plague was reported in the London parish of St Giles-in-the-Fields, just outside the western City wall. The disease — we now know it was bubonic plague spread by the fleas of black rats — would prove the worst outbreak London had seen in a generation. By August deaths were running at over 7,000 a week, the court had fled to Oxford, and the rich who could leave were leaving. The poor, tied to their parishes by the law, stayed.

Contemporary Explanations

Seventeenth-century Londoners had no germ theory. Most believed in miasma — foul air rising from rotting matter, drains and graveyards. Others blamed God’s judgement on a sinful city; clergy preached repentance and the king proclaimed days of fasting. Astrologers pointed to the comet seen in 1664 and to unusual conjunctions of the planets. Some accused Dutch spies. None of these explanations led to effective action against rats and fleas, the actual carriers, but the miasma theory did encourage useful measures such as burning fires, removing rotting refuse and avoiding crowds.

Key Fact

Contemporary Londoners explained the 1665 plague through miasma (bad air), divine punishment for sin, the comet of 1664 and unusual conjunctions of the planets. The outbreak peaked in August–September 1665 with over 7,000 burials a week recorded in the Bills of Mortality.

Bills of Mortality and the Records

London’s parishes had kept printed weekly Bills of Mortality since 1603. They listed deaths in each parish, broken down by reported cause. Older women paid as ‘searchers of the dead’ visited bodies and judged the cause — a poorly trained role open to bribery and error. The Bills probably underestimated plague deaths, because families paid searchers to record other causes (to avoid having their houses shut up) and because hundreds of Dissenters and Jews were buried outside the parish system. Modern historians estimate around 100,000 Londoners died, perhaps a fifth or a quarter of the city’s population.

Measures to Combat the Plague

The Lord Mayor and the Privy Council issued orders combining sensible precautions with desperate ones. Houses with infected residents were boarded up under guard, the door painted with a red cross and the words ‘Lord have mercy upon us’; the family was kept inside for forty days, often dying together. This practice of shutting up infected houses was deeply unpopular and probably accelerated deaths inside the affected households. Other measures targeted miasma: bonfires were lit in the streets, refuse was cleared, theatres and large gatherings were closed, and the city’s many stray dogs and cats were ordered killed (an order that almost certainly worsened the rat problem). Mass plague pits were dug at Aldgate, Finsbury and elsewhere as parish churchyards filled.

Each parish appointed a searcher of the dead, normally an older woman from the poorhouse. They were paid by the parish a few pence per body and were expected to inspect every corpse. The role was open to bribery: families paid them to record ‘fever’ or ‘consumption’ instead of plague, hoping to avoid the shutting-up order. Defoe’s later ‘Journal of the Plague Year’ (1722) is a fictional retelling but draws on real records and gives a vivid sense of how unreliable the system was.

Pepys, the Court and the Rich

Charles II and his court left for Salisbury in July 1665, then moved to Oxford for the autumn and winter. The wealthy who could afford it fled too, often to country estates. Samuel Pepys, the naval administrator, stayed in London for work and walked or boated to his office at the Navy Office while his family was sent to Greenwich. His diary records the streets growing ‘mighty empty’ and the panic of seeing crosses on doors. Around half of London’s clergy fled (the parishes worst affected often had their ministers leave); a number of Dissenter ministers, ejected in 1662, came back to fill the gap, preaching plague sermons in defiance of the Five Mile Act. The episode helped ease later attitudes to Dissenters in the City.

In late summer 1665 plague reached the Derbyshire village of Eyam, carried in a bundle of cloth sent up from London. The rector, William Mompesson, persuaded the villagers to quarantine themselves rather than flee and risk infecting neighbouring villages. Around 260 of the village’s 800 inhabitants died over fourteen months. Eyam is the most famous voluntary quarantine of the period and shows that plague was not only a London story; the disease followed trade routes into provincial towns and villages whose responses varied widely.

Results and Aftermath

The peak passed in October 1665. Cold weather killed off the fleas; surviving rats had built immunity. By February 1666 the king felt safe to return to Whitehall. The total death toll — around 100,000 from a population of roughly 460,000 — ranks the Great Plague of 1665 as one of the worst single demographic shocks in English urban history. Importantly, plague did not return on this scale. The 1665 outbreak was London’s last major plague epidemic, although why is still debated — better quarantine of shipping, the changing balance of rat species after the Fire, and the changing relationship between rats and humans in rebuilt brick housing have all been suggested. The Plague did NOT cause the Great Fire of 1666; nor did the Fire end the Plague, which had already declined sharply before the Fire began on 2 September 1666.

Key Fact

Around 100,000 Londoners died in the 1665 plague — perhaps a fifth or a quarter of the city. The plague was already declining sharply by August 1666 before the Great Fire began on 2 September; the Fire did not end the plague.

Examiners reward analytical narrative; lists of events with no causal explanation cap in the middle band. Avoid the common error of suggesting the Fire of 1666 ended the Plague: the Plague was already declining sharply by August 1666.

lessons.title: The Great Fire of London 1666: Disaster and Reconstruction

before.content_html:
Pudding Lane, 2 September 1666

Just after one o’clock in the morning of Sunday 2 September 1666, a fire broke out in the bakery of Thomas Farriner in Pudding Lane, near London Bridge. London had survived dozens of small fires; this one became the Great Fire. Three things made it different: a long dry summer that had baked the timber houses, an unusually strong easterly wind, and the densely packed warehouses near the Thames full of pitch, oil, hemp, brandy and coal — all highly flammable.

Bloodworth’s Fatal Indecision

When the Lord Mayor, Sir Thomas Bloodworth, was woken before dawn and asked to authorise the demolition of houses to make a firebreak, he reportedly snorted, ‘A woman might piss it out.’ By the time he changed his mind on Sunday afternoon, the wind had carried the fire halfway up Cannon Street. Houses in seventeenth-century London were timber-framed, jettied (each storey overhanging the one below), and packed against each other with thatch in poorer streets. Once a row caught, the whole row went up.

Key Fact

The Great Fire broke out at Thomas Farriner’s bakery in Pudding Lane in the early hours of 2 September 1666. Lord Mayor Bloodworth refused to authorise demolitions early enough; by the time he agreed, an easterly wind had spread the flames across the City.

The King and the Duke of York Take Charge

By Monday 3 September Charles II and his brother James, Duke of York, had taken personal command of firefighting from the Lord Mayor. They worked the leather-bucket lines themselves and authorised the use of gunpowder to blow up rows of houses ahead of the flames and create firebreaks. James personally directed gunpowder demolitions on Pudding Lane, Tower Street and elsewhere, and the king himself rode to Smithfield to organise water carts. Their visible leadership was politically important: Pepys recorded crowds cheering them, in marked contrast to royal absence during the Plague of the previous year.

The Scale of Destruction

By the time the fire died on Thursday 6 September, the cost was staggering. About four-fifths of the walled City was destroyed: 13,200 houses, 87 parish churches, the Royal Exchange, the Guildhall, the Custom House, four of the City’s gates and old St Paul’s Cathedral. Officially only six people died (the real toll was probably higher among the poor and uncounted). Around 70,000 of the City’s 80,000 inhabitants were made homeless overnight. They camped on Moorfields, Tower Hill and Lincoln’s Inn Fields. Charles II personally rode out to reassure the refugees.

The Second Dutch War was being fought, and Catholic France had recently joined the Dutch side. Many Londoners refused to believe a city could burn by accident. Stories spread of French and Dutch agents firing the city deliberately. A French watchmaker, Robert Hubert, confessed under questioning to starting the fire and was hanged at Tyburn in October 1666; the privy council itself privately doubted the confession (Hubert had been at sea on 2 September). The Monument to the Fire, completed in 1677, originally carried a Latin inscription blaming ‘the treachery and malice of the Popish faction’; it was chiselled off in the reign of James II and recut after 1689. The rumour that the Fire had been Catholic arson endured, feeding the Popish Plot panic of 1678.

The Rebuilding Acts

Within a fortnight Charles II had appointed a commission to plan reconstruction. Rebuilding Acts were passed in 1667 and 1670. They required all new houses to be built in brick and stone, not timber. Streets were widened and pavements added. House heights were standardised by class of street, with four set types of dwelling. The hearth tax was redirected to fund firefighting equipment, and a new tax on coal coming into the port of London was used to pay for the rebuilding of public buildings and parish churches.

Wren’s Plan and What Was Actually Built

Within days of the fire, the architect Sir Christopher Wren presented Charles II with a sweeping plan for a baroque London of broad avenues, piazzas and rationalised land plots. So did John Evelyn, Robert Hooke and others. None of these plans was adopted. The reason was simple: too many private freeholders held the medieval plots and the Crown had no money to compensate them. London was rebuilt on its old street pattern. Wren’s real triumph was the St Paul’s Cathedral (1675–1710) and 51 of the 87 lost parish churches, designed in his office between 1670 and 1700. Funded largely by a coal tax voted by Parliament, they gave the rebuilt City a unique horizon of white-stone steeples crowned by Wren’s dome.

Key Fact

The 1667 Rebuilding Act required houses to be built in brick or stone with standardised heights, on wider streets. Wren’s grand street plan was rejected because of private property rights, but he designed 51 new City churches and the new St Paul’s Cathedral, finished in 1710.

Samuel Pepys is the historian’s gift on the Fire. His diary entry for 2 September 1666 records being woken at three in the morning by his maid Jane to see the glow over the river. Pepys took a boat downstream to inspect the spread, returned to inform Charles II in person at Whitehall, and recorded the king’s order to demolish houses. Over the next four days he saved his own goods (including a parmesan cheese, famously buried in the garden), watched the fire from boats and rooftops and recorded conversations with refugees on Moorfields. Other eyewitnesses included John Evelyn, who walked through the smoking ruins on 7 September and recorded the heat of the stones rising through his shoes.

Effects on London

The Fire’s effects pulled in different directions. The trauma was real: thousands lost everything, and London paid for the reconstruction for forty years. But the rebuilt City was fireproof in a way the old one had not been; the Plague did not return on the 1665 scale, partly because brick and stone gave rats fewer hiding places; and Wren’s churches and cathedral became one of the world’s most admired urban skylines. The Fire also pushed wealthy Londoners west to Covent Garden, St James’s and the developing West End, accelerating a long-term shift in the city’s social geography. The Catholic arson rumour, meanwhile, refused to die, and would resurface in the Popish Plot panic of 1678.

Pull on Pudding Lane, Bloodworth, royal firefighting, the rebuilding acts, Wren’s churches and the Catholic arson rumour. Markers reward integrated argument with embedded source detail; describing the source then describing your own knowledge separately caps in the middle band.

lessons.title: The Catholic Question: Popish Plot and Rye House Plot

before.content_html:
A Country Primed for Panic

By 1678, English Protestants were jumpy. The fear of popery ran deep: France under Louis XIV was the dominant Catholic power, Charles II had signed the Treaty of Dover (1670) with French money attached, and his brother and heir — James, Duke of York — had openly become Catholic by 1673. Into that anxiety walked a disgraced Anglican clergyman called Titus Oates, with a story that would change the politics of the reign.

The Popish Plot, 1678

In the autumn of 1678 Oates and his collaborator, Israel Tonge, swore on oath before a London magistrate that Jesuits were planning to assassinate Charles II, replace him with his Catholic brother James, and re-impose Catholicism by force. Oates named priests, dates and meeting places; almost all of it was invented. But the plot acquired terrifying credibility on 17 October 1678, when the magistrate who had taken Oates’s deposition, Sir Edmund Berry Godfrey, was found dead on Primrose Hill, run through with his own sword.

Key Fact

The Popish Plot of 1678 was invented by Titus Oates and Israel Tonge. Although the assassination conspiracy was a fabrication, the unsolved murder of Sir Edmund Berry Godfrey on 17 October 1678 turned a wild story into a national emergency.

Oates fitted his lies to existing fears. Anti-Catholic feeling was reinforced by living memory of the Gunpowder Plot of 1605 and the Great Fire of 1666 (still rumoured to be a Catholic arson). Letters written by James’s secretary, Edward Coleman, to French Jesuits were genuinely incriminating about wider Catholic plans, even though Coleman knew nothing of the assassination story. When those letters were seized, they seemed to confirm Oates — and Coleman was hanged, drawn and quartered in December 1678.

Hysteria and Executions

Parliament passed the Second Test Act of 1678, barring Catholics from sitting in either House of Parliament — a clause aimed at James himself, who had to leave the Lords. Around 35 Catholics were executed between 1678 and 1681 on the basis of Oates’s perjury. They included Oliver Plunkett, the Catholic Archbishop of Armagh, hanged at Tyburn in 1681 and the last Catholic martyr executed in England. Catholics were ordered to leave London, and a wave of trials and pamphlets swept the country.

It was inside this hysteria that the Earl of Shaftesbury launched the Exclusion campaign to bar James from the throne — the subject of the next lesson. The Popish Plot is therefore the trigger for what historians now call the Exclusion Crisis: real political consequences flowed from a fictional conspiracy.

The Rye House Plot, 1683

The mood swung the other way after Charles II dissolved the Oxford Parliament in March 1681 and ruled without one. Frustrated Whig leaders began to consider violence. The Rye House Plot was a real conspiracy: a group of radicals planned to ambush Charles and James at Rye House, a moated farmhouse in Hertfordshire, on their journey home from the Newmarket races. A fire at Newmarket forced the king to leave early, the attack never happened, and one of the plotters — Josiah Keeling — informed the government in June 1683.

The reaction was severe. Lord William Russell was beheaded in July 1683, Algernon Sidney in December 1683; the Earl of Essex died in the Tower (officially suicide). The Duke of Monmouth fled to the Continent. Charles used the plot to purge corporations of Whig sympathisers, force boroughs to surrender their charters and rebuild their governments under Tory loyalists. By 1684 the Crown looked stronger than at any point since 1660.

Borough corporations elected MPs and ran local justice, so controlling them mattered for any future Parliament. Beginning with London in 1683, the government used quo warranto writs — legal challenges to a corporation’s charter — to force boroughs to surrender and accept new charters that gave the Crown a veto over key officers. By the time Charles died, more than fifty corporations had been remodelled. James II inherited a Parliament of constituencies stacked with Tories.

Key Fact

The Rye House Plot of 1683 was a real Whig conspiracy to assassinate Charles II and James, betrayed before it could be carried out. Russell and Sidney were executed, Monmouth fled abroad, and Charles used the plot to purge Whig corporations and govern without Parliament until his death in 1685.

Aftermath: A Reign Saved by a Lie and a Plot

The two episodes pull in opposite directions. The Popish Plot was an invention that nearly destroyed the monarchy; the Rye House Plot was real and ended up rescuing it. Together they show how raw fear of Catholic succession and republican conspiracy could be exploited by either side. Titus Oates was finally tried for perjury in 1685 under the new King James II, pilloried, whipped and imprisoned for life — though William of Orange would release him after the Glorious Revolution of 1688.

before.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Popish Plot of 1678 was a fabrication by Titus Oates and Israel Tonge, but the murder of Sir Edmund Berry Godfrey gave it terrifying credibility, leading to around 35 Catholic executions and the Second Test Act.
  • The Rye House Plot of 1683 was a real Whig conspiracy to assassinate Charles and James; its discovery led to the executions of Russell and Sidney and the flight of Monmouth.
  • Charles II used the Rye House revelations to purge corporations and rule without Parliament until his death in 1685, leaving the Crown stronger but the succession unresolved.

lessons.title: The Exclusion Crisis and the Succession

before.content_html:
A Childless King and a Catholic Heir

By the late 1670s the central political problem of Charles II’s reign was simple to state and impossible to solve: the king had no legitimate children, and the next in line was his openly Catholic brother. The hysteria of the Popish Plot turned that long-running anxiety into an emergency. The Earl of Shaftesbury and his allies in the House of Commons argued that Parliament had the right to alter the succession by statute and exclude James, Duke of York from the throne. Charles II disagreed.

The Three Exclusion Bills, 1679–1681

Three separate Parliaments tried to pass an Exclusion Bill. The first, in May 1679, passed its second reading in the Commons by 207 to 128 before Charles dissolved Parliament. A new election returned an even more anti-court House. The second Bill, late in 1680, passed the Commons but was thrown out by the Lords after a famous speech by the Earl of Halifax (a ‘trimmer’ who balanced the two sides). Charles called a third Parliament, deliberately moving it to royalist Oxford in March 1681; when the Commons reintroduced exclusion, he dissolved it after just one week.

Key Fact

Three Exclusion Bills (1679, 1680, 1681) tried to bar James from the throne. The first was lost to dissolution, the second to the House of Lords, and the third to the dissolution of the Oxford Parliament after only a week. Charles never summoned another Parliament.

Dissolving Parliament normally meant losing access to taxation. Charles could risk it because Louis XIV of France was secretly paying him a subsidy under a renewed agreement, and because the Crown’s finances had improved through the customs revenue from booming trade. Cash from France — about £385,000 between 1681 and 1685 — let Charles do without parliamentary supply for the rest of the reign. The choice to depend on Louis was politically risky but personally decisive.

Whigs and Tories: Two New Names

The Exclusion Crisis is the first time English politics divides cleanly into two named camps. Both names began as insults. Whig meant a Scottish cattle-thief, and was thrown at the exclusionists; Tory meant an Irish Catholic outlaw, and was thrown at the king’s defenders. Both stuck.

Whigs argued that Parliament had the right to determine the succession in order to preserve the Protestant religion and the rule of law; the strongest, in their view, were the constitutional rights settled in 1660. They drew support from Dissenters, London merchants and many of the gentry. Tories defended hereditary right as a gift of God, refused to accept that any subject could legally bar a lawful heir, and rallied to the Anglican Church and the loyalty oaths of 1660–65. They drew support from country squires, cathedral clergy and the universities.

The Monmouth Alternative

Some Whigs, including Shaftesbury, hoped to replace James with the Duke of Monmouth, Charles’s eldest illegitimate son. Monmouth was Protestant, popular, and a successful general at the Battle of Bothwell Bridge against Scottish Covenanters in 1679. He toured the country in 1680 to public cheers. But Charles refused absolutely to acknowledge any marriage to Monmouth’s mother, Lucy Walter, and would not legitimise him. Monmouth was effectively sidelined by 1681 and would later return to lead an unsuccessful rebellion in 1685.

Whig pamphlets, including Andrew Marvell’s anonymous ‘Account of the Growth of Popery and Arbitrary Government’ (1677), painted exclusion as the only safeguard against tyranny. Tory replies, including Sir Robert Filmer’s ‘Patriarcha’ (published 1680, written earlier), argued that royal authority descended from Adam and could not be conditioned on religion. The same arguments would be answered after the reign by John Locke’s ‘Two Treatises of Government’ (1689), drafted in part during the Exclusion years. Top-band answers can use these sources to show that the Crisis was a contest of ideas as well as politics.

The Oxford Parliament and Tory Reaction

The dissolution of the Oxford Parliament on 28 March 1681 is the turning point. Charles read out a printed declaration justifying his action and had it sent to every parish church to be read after the sermon. Public opinion swung. Tory loyal addresses flooded in from the corporations. Shaftesbury was acquitted of treason in November 1681 by a London grand jury (London still had a Whig sheriff), but the political tide had turned. He fled to Holland in 1682 and died there. Charles ruled without Parliament for the remaining four years of his life.

Key Fact

The Exclusion Crisis produced the first English party division. Whigs argued Parliament could alter the succession to keep England Protestant; Tories defended hereditary right and the Anglican settlement. The labels were originally insults, and the same divide would resurface in 1688 and beyond.

lessons.title: Restoration Stage, Coffee Houses and Women in Public Life

before.content_html:
From Closed Theatres to Royal Patents

In 1642 the Puritan Parliament had ordered London’s theatres closed; in 1660 Charles II reopened them. He did so by issuing two royal letters patent, granting a near-monopoly on professional drama in London to two companies: the King’s Company under Thomas Killigrew, and the Duke’s Company under William Davenant. For most of the reign, only these two licensed playhouses could perform new spoken drama. Theatre was therefore not an open market — it was a piece of court patronage.

Women on the Stage from 1660–61

A second royal letter, issued by Charles in 1662, made it explicit: women’s parts were to be played by women. Before 1660, female roles had been performed by boys. The first known professional actress on the public English stage was probably Margaret Hughes, playing Desdemona in ‘Othello’ on 8 December 1660. Within a few years a generation of star actresses — including Nell Gwyn, who became Charles II’s mistress, and Elizabeth Barry, the leading tragedienne of the next generation — was working full-time in London.

Key Fact

In 1660 Charles II granted patents to the King’s Company (Killigrew) and the Duke’s Company (Davenant), creating a two-theatre monopoly in London. From December 1660 women played female roles professionally for the first time in English history.

Restoration Comedy

Restoration comedy was the period’s defining new genre. Plays such as Etherege’s ‘The Man of Mode’ (1676), Wycherley’s ‘The Country Wife’ (1675) and Congreve’s ‘The Way of the World’ (1700) used witty dialogue, sexual intrigue and satire of fashionable London society. The plots were often bawdy, the characters self-aware, and the audience overwhelmingly drawn from the elite. Theatres were small (around 700 seats), candlelit, and rowdy; the king himself often attended, sometimes accompanied by his mistresses.

Female playwrights also broke through. Aphra Behn became the first English woman to make a living from writing. Her plays — ‘The Rover’ (1677) is the most famous — were box-office successes; her novel ‘Oroonoko’ (1688), an early prose narrative about an enslaved African prince, has been read ever since. Behn was attacked for her sex (Pope later sneered that ‘the stage how loosely does Astrea tread’), but she earned, lived independently, and is buried in Westminster Abbey.

A typical performance began at 3:30 p.m. and lasted around three hours. Audiences ate oranges (sold by ‘orange-girls’ — Nell Gwyn famously started as one) and chatted through the play. The pit, occupied by gentlemen and writers, faced raked seating in the boxes. New plays alternated with revivals of Shakespeare in heavily adapted forms: William Davenant rewrote ‘Macbeth’ with singing witches, and Nahum Tate gave ‘King Lear’ a happy ending in 1681 that held the stage for over 150 years. Spectacle and scenery — new movable flats, lit by candles — meant Restoration theatre looked very different from the bare Globe of Shakespeare’s day.

Coffee Houses: London’s Penny Universities

The first London coffee house had opened in 1652, before the Restoration; by the 1670s the city had over 80, by 1700 several hundred. A coffee house was open to any man who could pay a penny for a dish of coffee. Newspapers were laid out free, gossip and political news circulated, and many trades clustered around particular houses: Lloyd’s in Lombard Street became the centre of marine insurance, Jonathan’s the heart of stock-jobbing in the City. Contemporaries called them penny universities because the conversation was an education for the price of a drink.

Charles II disliked them. In December 1675 he issued a royal proclamation suppressing coffee houses on the grounds that they encouraged sedition and idleness. The reaction was immediate: shopkeepers, customers and judges objected, and the proclamation was withdrawn within days. The episode shows both the perceived political power of the coffee houses and the limits of royal control over public opinion.

Coffee houses were almost always male spaces: women normally entered only as servers or as the wives running the business. A 1674 satirical pamphlet, ‘The Women’s Petition Against Coffee’, mocked husbands for spending all day talking politics rather than at home; an answering ‘Men’s Petition’ replied in kind. The exclusion of women from this central new public space contrasts sharply with the new visibility of actresses on the stage and shows that the ‘public sphere’ opened up unevenly.

The Status of Women

For most women the legal framework remained the doctrine of coverture: a married woman could not own property, sign contracts or sue in her own right. But the visible gains were real. Actresses became celebrities; female playwrights and poets such as Aphra Behn and Katherine Philips earned by their writing; women published in print on religion (the Quaker Margaret Fell argued for women’s right to preach); and royal mistresses such as Barbara Villiers and Louise de Kéroualle exerted real political influence at court. Restoration culture is therefore a story of widened public visibility against unchanged underlying law — a tension worth holding in any answer about women’s status.

Key Fact

Coffee houses charged a penny for entry and offered free newspapers, becoming the engine of news, business and political talk. Charles II tried to ban them in December 1675 but withdrew the proclamation within days under public pressure.

Markers reward both timescales explicitly.

lessons.title: The Royal Society, Pepys and the New Science

before.content_html:
A Lecture at Gresham College, November 1660

On the evening of Wednesday 28 November 1660, twelve men stayed behind after a lecture by the young astronomer Christopher Wren at Gresham College in the City of London. They agreed to form a club for promoting ‘Physico-Mathematicall Experimentall Learning’. The group built on years of informal meetings — some at Wadham College Oxford under John Wilkins during the Civil War — but the November 1660 meeting is now treated as the founding of the Royal Society.

The Royal Charter, 1662

Charles II granted the new body its first Royal Charter on 15 July 1662, with a second, more detailed charter the next year. The full title was ‘The Royal Society of London for Improving Natural Knowledge’. The king became its patron, presenting fellows with a silver mace that they still carry today. Crucially, royal patronage was honour, not money. Fellows paid their own subscriptions of one shilling a week, and from 1672 each new member paid a forty-shilling admission fee. The Crown gave no Treasury funding. This is why the modern misconception that the Society was a government department is wrong: it was a private subscription club with the king’s blessing.

Key Fact

The Royal Society was chartered by Charles II in July 1662. Its full title was ‘The Royal Society of London for Improving Natural Knowledge’. It was a private subscription society funded by its fellows’ weekly dues, not by the Treasury — royal patronage was prestige, not money.

Wilkins, Boyle, Hooke, Wren

The early Society’s leadership reads like a roll-call of the new science. John Wilkins, the Warden of Wadham College Oxford, ran the original wartime experimental club. Robert Boyle, the wealthy Irish son of the Earl of Cork, used his Oxford laboratory to work on what we now call Boyle’s Law of gases (published 1662). His paid assistant Robert Hooke became the Society’s first Curator of Experiments in 1662, demonstrating new effects at every weekly meeting; his ‘Micrographia’ (1665) showed the world the first detailed microscope drawings of insects, cork cells and snowflakes. Christopher Wren, the astronomer who triggered the founding meeting, became Surveyor of the King’s Works in 1669 and shifted the centre of his work towards architecture without leaving the Society. Natural philosophy was the period’s name for what we would now call physical science.

Each Wednesday afternoon Hooke would prepare an experiment, often involving Boyle’s air pump, magnetic effects, blood transfusion or telescope observation. Fellows took turns to read papers, often in Latin, and to repeat each other’s experiments — the principle that scientific claims must be reproduced before being accepted is one of the Society’s lasting contributions to method. From 1665 the secretary Henry Oldenburg edited ‘Philosophical Transactions’, the first English-language scientific journal still published today. The motto ‘Nullius in verba’ (‘Take nobody’s word for it’) summed up the experimental ideal.

Pepys, the Society and Newton’s Principia

Samuel Pepys was elected a fellow on 15 February 1665. Reformer of the Navy by day, he kept his diary at night and gave the Society advice on naval matters. He was elected President in December 1684, a year before the death of Charles II, and he held the chair until 1686. In that capacity he gave the formal imprimatur — a licence to print — to Isaac Newton’s ‘Principia Mathematica’ (full Latin title: ‘Philosophiae Naturalis Principia Mathematica’), published 5 July 1687. The book set out the laws of motion and universal gravitation that defined modern physics for the next two and a half centuries. Pepys’s name appears on the title page as President of the Society.

Wren beyond St Paul’s

Wren’s scientific career flowed into his architectural one. In 1675 Charles II commissioned him to build the Royal Observatory at Greenwich, with John Flamsteed as the first Astronomer Royal. Its purpose was practical: accurate star charts to help English ships find longitude at sea. Wren also designed the Royal Hospital at Chelsea (1682) for old soldiers, the Trinity College Library at Cambridge (1676), and the new buildings at Kensington Palace and Hampton Court for William and Mary after the reign. Architecture and the new science met in Wren personally — he understood the geometry of his domes because he understood astronomy.

The early Society was as quarrelsome as it was inventive. Robert Hooke and Isaac Newton clashed bitterly in 1672 over the nature of light and again in the 1680s over priority on the inverse-square law of gravitation. Hooke believed Newton had drawn on his own earlier ideas about gravity without credit; Newton, when President from 1703, removed every reference to Hooke from the Society’s rooms and possibly arranged for Hooke’s portrait to be lost. Disputes over priority were typical of seventeenth-century natural philosophy — the Society’s journal ‘Philosophical Transactions’ was partly designed to settle them by recording who published what first.

Royal Patronage of the Arts

Patronage of science was part of a wider royal cultural policy. Charles II refounded the Royal Library, founded the Royal Mathematical School at Christ’s Hospital in 1673 to train navigators, supported musicians like Henry Purcell at the Chapel Royal, and used Sir Peter Lely (court painter from 1661) to produce the famous ‘Windsor Beauties’ portrait series. The pattern was the same as in science: the Crown gave prestige, names and a few salaries; the City of London and private patrons paid most of the bills.

Key Fact

Robert Hooke was the Royal Society’s first Curator of Experiments and demonstrated weekly experiments at Gresham College. Samuel Pepys, elected fellow in 1665 and President from 1684, gave the imprimatur to Isaac Newton’s ‘Principia’ in 1687.
before.exam_tip_html: For an ‘Explain Significance’ question on royal patronage of science, structure your answer in two halves. Significance at the time: the 1662 Charter gave the new society prestige and access without the Crown having to pay for it; this was a model the Treasury could afford and that fellows could fund. Significance over time: it produced an institution that has continuously published scientific work since 1665 and gave its imprimatur to Newton’s ‘Principia’ in 1687. Avoid the common error of saying the Crown funded the Society — royal patronage was prestige, not Treasury cash.
