practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the early Royal Society.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• It grew out of a Gresham College meeting in November 1660 after a lecture by Christopher Wren and was granted its first Royal Charter by Charles II in July 1662.
• It was a private subscription society funded by fellows’ weekly dues, not by the Treasury, despite the king’s patronage and the silver mace he presented.
• It met weekly at Gresham College, with Robert Hooke as Curator of Experiments demonstrating air-pump, microscope and astronomical effects.
• Its secretary Henry Oldenburg edited ‘Philosophical Transactions’ from 1665, the first English-language scientific journal still in publication.
[4 marks — 2 marks per feature: 1 for identification, 2 for development.]

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of Charles II’s patronage of the arts and sciences.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• He chartered the Royal Society in 1662, gave it a silver mace and made the king its formal patron, but provided no Treasury funding.
• He founded the Royal Observatory at Greenwich in 1675, with John Flamsteed as the first Astronomer Royal, to produce accurate star charts for navigation.
• He founded the Royal Mathematical School at Christ’s Hospital in 1673 to train navigators for the navy and merchant fleet.
• He commissioned Sir Peter Lely as court painter from 1661 and supported the composer Henry Purcell at the Chapel Royal.
[4 marks — 2 marks per feature: 1 for identification, 2 for development.]

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of the Royal Society’s 1662 Royal Charter on the development of English science.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• It gave the loose Gresham College meeting a corporate identity, allowing it to hold property, choose officers and admit fellows formally.
• Its ‘Nullius in verba’ motto and the practice of repeating each other’s experiments embedded the principle of reproducibility at the heart of English natural philosophy.
• Its journal ‘Philosophical Transactions’ (1665) created a permanent printed record of experimental work, accessible to scientists across Europe.
• It allowed the Society to give the imprimatur in 1687 to Isaac Newton’s ‘Principia Mathematica’, the foundational text of modern physics.

Mastering: Multiple effects developed with named individuals and causal chains.
Secure: Two or more effects with relevant detail.
Developing: Effects identified, limited explanation.
Emerging: Simple statements; effects unclear.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of royal patronage for the development of the Royal Society.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time, royal patronage gave the new Society prestige, legal personality and the king’s mace; it allowed fellows to claim authority for their experimental method against rivals.
• The Royal Charter let the Society admit fellows from across Europe, building an international scientific reputation that would otherwise have been impossible.
• Royal patronage came without Treasury funding, so the Society had to live on subscriptions; this kept it independent of changing royal policy and protected it through later political storms.
• Significance over time: the Society outlasted the dynasty that founded it; it continuously published ‘Philosophical Transactions’ from 1665 and gave the imprimatur to Newton’s ‘Principia’ in 1687, helping to make English science world-leading by 1700.

Mastering: Significance shown both at the time and over time, with precise examples.
Secure: Clear significance explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Some significance with limited examples.
Emerging: Simple description; significance unclear.

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of Samuel Pepys’s presidency of the Royal Society in the mid-1680s.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• It tied the Society to the practical needs of naval administration: Pepys had reformed Royal Navy victualling and shipbuilding and used Society contacts on technical questions.
• It gave the Society a President with court access at exactly the moment Newton’s ‘Principia’ needed institutional backing to be printed.
• Pepys gave the imprimatur to the ‘Principia Mathematica’ in 1687, signing his name on the title page as President and giving the book the Society’s formal endorsement.
• It demonstrated that the Society could survive the death of its royal patron Charles II in 1685 and the political crisis around James II without losing its scientific role.

Mastering: Multiple effects developed with named individuals and causal chains.
Secure: Two or more effects with relevant detail.
Developing: Effects identified, limited explanation.
Emerging: Simple statements; effects unclear.

practice_questions.text: Argue, using the evidence of 1660–1687, that the Royal Society’s independence from the Crown — rather than royal patronage itself — was the most important reason for its scientific success. Discuss funding, membership and continuity.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
• The Society was funded by fellows’ subscriptions, not by the Treasury, so it could choose its own experiments and admit foreign fellows without political interference.
• Independence allowed it to publish ‘Philosophical Transactions’ freely from 1665 and to give the imprimatur to Newton’s ‘Principia’ in 1687, even as the political climate shifted under James II.
• Membership reached far beyond court: Boyle was a wealthy private patron, Hooke a salaried curator, and many fellows were merchants, ship’s captains and physicians outside the royal household.

Arguments to weigh against:
• Royal patronage gave the Society its prestige, its mace and its legal corporate status, without which it could not have admitted fellows or held property.
• Charles II personally founded the Royal Observatory in 1675 and the Royal Mathematical School in 1673, both of which fed practical work back into the Society.
• Without the king’s 1662 Charter, the Gresham College group would have been one Oxford–London circle among many and might never have outlasted its founders.

A strong response weighs independence against patronage, and reaches a substantiated overall judgement — for example, that prestige came from the Crown but durability came from the subscription model.

Mastering: Substantiated overall judgement, both sides developed, precise terminology.
Secure: Clear argument with both sides covered.
Developing: One side developed more than the other.
Emerging: Descriptive with limited argument.
[16 marks + 4 SPaG]

lessons.title: Sea Power, the Navigation Acts and the Dutch Wars

before.content_html:
Mercantilism: A Zero-Sum World

Mercantilism shaped Restoration economic policy. Its core assumption was that the world’s wealth was fixed: one nation’s gain in trade was another nation’s loss. To prosper, a nation must export more than it imported, hoard precious metal (bullion), found colonies that supplied raw materials and bought back finished goods, and protect its trade with monopoly chartered companies. The Dutch Republic, with its tiny population and vast trading fleet, was the model and the rival: by 1660 the Dutch carried more freight by tonnage than every other European nation combined.

The Navigation Acts

The first Navigation Acts had been passed in 1651 by the Commonwealth, but the Restoration Parliament strengthened them. The Act of 1660 required that goods carried to or from English colonies must travel in ships built and owned in England or its colonies, with English masters and three-quarters English crews. The Act listed ‘enumerated’ goods — sugar, tobacco, cotton, ginger, dyestuffs — that could only be sent to England, even if their final market was elsewhere. The Staple Act of 1663 added that European goods bound for the colonies must first be landed in an English port and pay duties before re-export. The Act of 1673 added export duties on those colonial goods sent direct between colonies.

Key Fact

The Navigation Acts of 1660, 1663 and 1673 required colonial trade to use English or colonial ships, listed enumerated goods (sugar, tobacco, cotton) that must land in England, and forced European goods bound for the colonies through English ports. Their target was Dutch shipping.

The Second Dutch War, 1665–67

The first major conflict came in 1665. England declared war over trade rivalry, the seizure of New Amsterdam (renamed New York in honour of the Duke of York) the year before, and skirmishes off West Africa. Early English success at the Battle of Lowestoft on 3 June 1665 — in which the Dutch flagship blew up — gave way to disease and money problems on the English fleet through 1666. In June 1667 the war ended in humiliation: Admiral Michiel de Ruyter sailed up the river Medway, broke the chain at Chatham and burned much of the English fleet at anchor. The flagship ‘Royal Charles’ was towed back to the Netherlands as a trophy. The Medway raid was the worst defeat in English naval history.

The Treaty of Breda and Pepys’s Reforms

The war ended at the Treaty of Breda in July 1667. Under it England kept New York and New Jersey; the Dutch kept Suriname and the spice island of Run; both sides relaxed the Navigation Acts slightly to ease trade. The political fallout was severe: Edward Hyde, Earl of Clarendon, was impeached and fled to France in November 1667. Samuel Pepys, the naval administrator, used the post-war period to push through reforms of naval victualling, of pay and of shipbuilding contracts. New ships of the line were ordered, the dockyards at Chatham, Portsmouth and Plymouth were upgraded, and a coherent system of naval administration began to emerge.

Naval battles in the Restoration moved from chaotic mêlées to disciplined formations. Under line of battle tactics, fleets sailed in a single column so that every ship’s broadside cannon could fire on the enemy line in turn. The English Fighting Instructions of 1653 had codified the tactic, and the Restoration navy refined it. Ships were classified into six rates by gun count; the largest, the three-decked ‘ship of the line’, carried 90 to 100 guns. Pepys’s shipbuilding programme of the 1670s and 1680s created the early ships of the line that would fight under William III against Louis XIV in the 1690s.

The Third Dutch War, 1672–74

Five years after the Medway humiliation, Charles II went to war on the Dutch again — this time as Louis XIV’s ally under the secret Treaty of Dover. The Third Dutch War began in 1672. The English fleet under James, Duke of York fought De Ruyter at Solebay in May 1672 to a bloody draw. On land, the French overran the Dutch Republic, but the Dutch broke the dykes to flood the country and held out. Parliament was furious about both the Catholic alliance with France and the costs of the war. In 1674 it forced Charles to make a separate peace at the Second Treaty of Westminster, two years before France finished its own war. The political effect was significant: Parliament had used the power of the purse to override royal foreign policy, and Charles never again pushed an open military alliance with France.

Spain and France framed Charles II’s naval policy throughout. Spain remained the old enemy of the Cromwellian period, but its empire was visibly declining and its main use to England was as the source of the privateering commissions that legitimised raids on its Caribbean colonies. France was the rising danger: Louis XIV’s navy, built up by Colbert from 1661, grew from twenty ships to over 270 by the 1680s. Charles II danced between the two: he allied with France against the Dutch under the Treaty of Dover, but was forced by Parliament to sign the Triple Alliance with the Dutch and Sweden against France in 1668. By the end of the reign Parliament feared France far more than it feared Spain — a shift that would define William III’s wars against Louis after 1689.

Effects of the Wars

Despite the Medway disaster, English shipping grew strongly across the reign. By the 1680s the English merchant fleet was approaching the size of the Dutch and pulling ahead in colonial routes. The Navigation Acts shifted carrying-trade business from Dutch shippers to English ones. Sugar imports from the Caribbean, tobacco from Virginia and Maryland, and African gold and slaves from West Africa increasingly travelled in English bottoms. The customs revenue from this booming trade was what kept Charles II solvent during his rule without Parliament after 1681. Pepys’s naval reforms left a stronger navy and a working dockyard system. The age of Dutch maritime dominance was ending.

Key Fact

The Second Dutch War (1665–67) ended in humiliation at the Medway, where De Ruyter burned the English fleet at Chatham. The Third Dutch War (1672–74) was fought as Louis XIV’s ally; Parliament forced peace at Westminster in 1674.
before.exam_tip_html: For an ‘8 marks — Explain Effects’ question on the Navigation Acts, build chains: identify an effect (e.g. Dutch carrying-trade was excluded from English colonies), explain why it mattered (English merchants captured the freight business), then link to a wider consequence (English shipping grew strongly and customs revenue helped Charles II rule without Parliament after 1681). Develop two distinct effects, not one effect at length. Avoid drifting into general descriptions of mercantilism — markers reward consequences, not background.

lessons.title: Empire, Slavery and the End of the Reign 1685

before.content_html:
Catherine of Braganza’s Dowry, 1662

When Charles II married Catherine of Braganza in 1662, her dowry was a turning point in English overseas expansion. The cash — around £360,000 — mattered, but the territory mattered more. The dowry transferred Bombay (modern Mumbai) and Tangier on the North African coast to the English Crown, and gave English merchants trading rights in Brazil and the Portuguese East Indies. England suddenly held two strategic harbours on key world trade routes. Tangier guarded the entrance to the Mediterranean. Bombay opened a deep-water Indian port. Both would shape English imperial reach for the next two centuries.

The East India Company and Bombay

Charles II handed the Crown’s new Bombay possession to the East India Company in 1668 in return for an annual rent of £10. The Company already operated factories at Surat, Madras and on the coasts of Java and Sumatra. With Bombay it gained a fortified port directly under its control. By a series of charters in the 1670s and 1680s the Company received near-sovereign powers in its Indian territories: it could fortify, mint money, raise its own troops, hold courts, declare war on non-Christian princes and make peace. By 1685 the Company maintained around 700 European soldiers in India and the beginnings of an Indian sepoy army. The political form of the British Empire as a chartered company governing for profit was being put in place.

Key Fact

Catherine of Braganza’s 1662 dowry brought Bombay and Tangier to the English Crown. In 1668 Charles II handed Bombay to the East India Company for an annual rent of £10; later charters gave it near-sovereign powers including its own troops, courts and currency.

Tangier: A Costly North African Outpost

Tangier was the dowry’s expensive failure. Held against constant attacks from the Moroccan ruler Mawlay Ismaíl, it required a permanent English garrison and a large mole (a stone breakwater) which Pepys oversaw on a 1683 inspection visit. The cost ran to roughly £1.5 million across the reign — comparable to the entire annual royal income. In 1684 Charles ordered the garrison evacuated and the mole blown up to deny it to the Moroccans. Tangier showed both the temptation and the trap of mid-century empire: prestige territory could be ruinously expensive to hold without a sustainable trade purpose.

Hudson Bay and the Fur Trade

In May 1670 Charles II chartered the Hudson’s Bay Company, granting it trading rights and quasi-governmental powers over the entire watershed of Hudson Bay — an area roughly the size of Western Europe, named ‘Rupert’s Land’ after the king’s cousin Prince Rupert, the Company’s first governor. The Company built fur-trading posts at Fort Charles, Fort Nelson and elsewhere, exchanging European goods (axes, kettles, cloth, guns) with Cree and other First Nations peoples for beaver pelts. The North American fur trade tied a vast new region into the English economy and competed directly with the French in Canada. The Hudson’s Bay Company is the oldest commercial company still operating in continuous existence in North America.

Cromwell had seized Jamaica from Spain in 1655 as part of the ‘Western Design’. Charles II kept it. By the 1670s Jamaica had become the centre of two profitable English ventures: sugar plantations worked by enslaved Africans, and Caribbean privateering. The most famous privateer was the Welsh-born privateer Captain Henry Morgan, who attacked Spanish settlements under commissions from the governor of Jamaica. In 1671 Morgan led around 1,400 men across the isthmus of Panama, sacking Panama City and burning it to the ground. London arrested him to placate the Spanish but quietly knighted him in 1674 and made him Lieutenant-Governor of Jamaica from 1674. The line between piracy and policy was very thin under Charles II.

The Royal African Company and the Slave Trade

The reign also brought the English state into the transatlantic slave trade on a new scale. The Royal African Company was first chartered in 1660 as the ‘Company of Royal Adventurers’, and refounded in 1672 with James, Duke of York as governor and Charles II as a major shareholder. Between 1672 and 1685 the Company shipped roughly 90,000 enslaved Africans across the Atlantic. People bought by the Company were branded with the Duke of York’s initials ‘DY’ on the chest. The trade now flowed through royally chartered companies with the Crown as a shareholder — a major escalation from earlier private slaving voyages. By the 1680s the slave trade was the single most lucrative English overseas enterprise.

By 1680 sugar had overtaken tobacco as the most valuable English colonial import, with Jamaica and Barbados between them producing the bulk of supply. Plantations were worked by enslaved Africans shipped under Royal African Company contracts. The economic logic was brutal: a sugar mill needed dozens of skilled and unskilled workers continuously, and the planter class settled on a coerced workforce because indentured European labour was scarce, expensive and unwilling to do field work in tropical heat. By 1685 enslaved Africans outnumbered white settlers on Jamaica by roughly four to one. Profits flowed to London merchants, planters and the Royal Treasury through customs duties on sugar imports.

The Last Years of the Reign 1681–85

Charles II ruled without Parliament from March 1681 until his death. Customs revenue from the booming colonial trade kept the Crown solvent, supplemented by Louis XIV’s subsidy of around £385,000. The Tory reaction after the Rye House Plot in 1683 left him politically unchallenged. By 1685 the Treasury had run a small surplus in the previous year. Charles II died on 6 February 1685, after suffering an apoplectic fit four days earlier. On his deathbed he received Catholic last rites secretly from the priest John Huddleston. The succession passed peacefully to his Catholic brother — James II.

The Reign in Review

Charles II’s twenty-five years had transformed England’s position in the world. England now held Bombay, the Hudson Bay watershed and Jamaica; it had survived the Plague, the Fire and three wars with the Dutch; it had founded the Royal Society and rebuilt the City under Wren. Less happily, the Catholic succession was unresolved, the slave trade had become a state-backed enterprise, and the religious tensions of the Civil War had been postponed rather than solved. James II would inherit a strong Crown and a fragile country. The Glorious Revolution of 1688 was already implicit in the unfinished business of his brother’s reign.

Key Fact

Three chartered companies drove English overseas expansion under Charles II: the East India Company (Bombay 1668), the Royal African Company (West Africa 1660/1672) and the Hudson’s Bay Company (Rupert’s Land 1670). All three combined trading monopolies with quasi-governmental powers.
before.exam_tip_html: For an ‘Explain Significance’ question on the slave trade under Charles II, structure your answer in two halves. Significance at the time: the Royal African Company shipped around 90,000 enslaved Africans across the Atlantic between 1672 and 1685, with the Duke of York as governor and the king as a shareholder — making the slave trade a state-backed enterprise. Significance over time: it normalised state involvement in the trade for over a century, fed the sugar plantations of Jamaica and Barbados, and underwrote the wealth that paid for much of late-Stuart London. Markers reward both timescales explicitly.

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of the slave trade on English wealth and empire under Charles II.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• It made the Royal African Company one of the most profitable chartered companies of the period, with around 90,000 enslaved Africans shipped across the Atlantic between 1672 and 1685.
• It tied the English state directly into the trade through the king’s shareholding and James’s governorship, normalising state-backed slaving for the next century.
• It supplied the labour force for the sugar plantations of Jamaica and Barbados, generating customs revenue that helped finance Charles II’s rule without Parliament after 1681.
• It established the slave-trading network of forts on the West African coast (Cape Coast Castle and others) which would underwrite English commercial dominance in the eighteenth century.

Mastering: Multiple effects developed with named individuals and causal chains.
Secure: Two or more effects with relevant detail.
Developing: Effects identified, limited explanation.
Emerging: Simple statements; effects unclear.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the Hudson’s Bay Company charter of 1670 for English overseas expansion.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time, it gave England a chartered claim to the entire Hudson Bay watershed — an area named ‘Rupert’s Land’ after Prince Rupert, the Company’s first governor and the king’s cousin.
• It established a fur-trading network with Cree and other First Nations peoples, bringing beaver pelts into the English economy and challenging French dominance in Canada.
• Significance over time: the Hudson’s Bay Company is the oldest continuously operating commercial company in North America and its 1670 charter underpinned English claims to most of modern Canada.
• It established the model of a chartered company governing vast non-European territory with quasi-governmental powers, a model copied for the East India Company and Royal African Company.

Mastering: Significance shown both at the time and over time, with precise examples.
Secure: Clear significance explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Some significance with limited examples.
Emerging: Simple description; significance unclear.

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of Catherine of Braganza’s 1662 dowry on English overseas reach.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• It brought Bombay (modern Mumbai) to the English Crown, which Charles II handed to the East India Company in 1668 as the foundation of English Indian power.
• It brought Tangier on the North African coast, which guarded the entrance to the Mediterranean; the cost of holding it ran to roughly £1.5 million across the reign before evacuation in 1684.
• It gave English merchants trading rights in Brazil and the Portuguese East Indies, opening new commercial opportunities.
• It allied England with Portugal against Spain, supporting Portuguese independence and English Atlantic and Indian Ocean trade.

Mastering: Multiple effects developed with named individuals and causal chains.
Secure: Two or more effects with relevant detail.
Developing: Effects identified, limited explanation.
Emerging: Simple statements; effects unclear.

practice_questions.text: Argue, using the evidence of 1660–1685, that the rise of chartered trading companies — rather than royal patronage of culture or naval reform — was the most important development of Charles II’s reign for England’s long-term position in the world. Discuss the East India Company, the Royal African Company and the Hudson’s Bay Company.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
• The East India Company, granted Bombay in 1668 and near-sovereign powers in its Indian territories, became the institutional vehicle of British rule in India for the next two centuries.
• The Royal African Company under James, Duke of York normalised state-backed slaving and built the West African fort network that anchored English commerce in the eighteenth century.
• The Hudson’s Bay Company chartered in 1670 created an English claim to most of modern Canada and is still operating, the longest-lived such company in North American history.

Arguments to weigh against:
• Pepys’s naval reforms after 1668 created the first generation of English ships of the line, without which the chartered companies could not have been protected.
• Royal patronage of the arts and sciences (Royal Society 1662, Royal Observatory 1675) gave English science and architecture an enduring world-leading reputation.
• The Tory reaction after 1681 and the strong financial position Charles II left to James II shaped the political landscape that the Glorious Revolution would then reorder.

A strong response weighs companies against navy and culture, and reaches a substantiated overall judgement — for example, that the chartered company model was the most enduring institutional legacy because it was still governing in 1857 (East India Company) and beyond.

Mastering: Substantiated overall judgement, both sides developed, precise terminology.
Secure: Clear argument with both sides covered.
Developing: One side developed more than the other.
Emerging: Descriptive with limited argument.
[16 marks + 4 SPaG]

lessons.title: The Dutch Raid on the Medway: Historic Environment 2027

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Medway's defences in June 1667.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• The fort at Sheerness covering the river mouth — still unfinished and weakly garrisoned, it fell to a Dutch landing on 10 June.
• The iron chain across the river at Gillingham, floated on stages and supported by shore batteries and guardships — broken on 12 June because its supporting defences were under-crewed.
• Upnor Castle, the Elizabethan gun fort facing the Chatham moorings, which mounted the stiffest resistance of the raid.
• The river itself: a winding, shoal-banked channel navigable for great ships only on the tide with expert pilots.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the condition of the English fleet at Chatham in 1667.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• The great ships were laid up — moored without full crews, stores or rigging — as a deliberate economy by a bankrupt government.
• Skeleton crews and unpaid men: sailors held tickets instead of wages, morale had collapsed, and some English seamen actually served the Dutch as pilots.
• The flagship Royal Charles lay at her moorings so lightly manned that a Dutch boarding party took her almost without a fight.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the Crown's financial problems for the success of the Dutch raid on the Medway.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Money explains the target existing at all: the battle fleet was laid up because Plague, Fire and two years of war had emptied the treasury.
• Money explains each defensive failure: Sheerness unfinished, the chain's batteries without platforms or gunners, guardships undermanned.
• Money explains the pilots: seamen paid in worthless tickets deserted, and some guided the Dutch through the shoals — the river's natural defence sold off by neglect.
• The raid then deepened the crisis it exposed, forcing peace at Breda on Dutch terms.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of the Dutch raid on the Medway, 10–14 June 1667.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• 10 June: De Ruyter's fleet, with Cornelis de Witt aboard, lands at Sheerness; the unfinished fort falls and the river mouth is lost.
• 12 June: working upriver on the tide with expert pilots, the Dutch break the chain at Gillingham, burn the guardships and capture the Royal Charles.
• 13 June: under fire from Upnor Castle and shore batteries, fireships burn the Royal Oak, Loyal London and Royal James at their moorings.
• 14 June and after: the Dutch withdraw with the tide, towing the Royal Charles, and blockade the Thames for weeks; roughly a dozen warships have been lost, some scuttled by the defenders themselves.

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of the Medway raid on Restoration England.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Immediate panic: invasion rumours in London, runs on the goldsmiths, Pepys sending his wife and gold to safety — a collapse of confidence in the government.
• Political consequences: Peter Pett scapegoated and sent to the Tower; Clarendon driven from office into exile by the autumn.
• Diplomatic consequences: the Treaty of Breda signed in July 1667 on terms England could no longer contest.
• Naval consequences: root-and-branch rebuilding of the Medway defences (including a proper fort at Sheerness) and reform of naval administration, in which Pepys's office was central.

practice_questions.text: 'The Dutch succeeded on the Medway because of English neglect rather than Dutch skill.' How far does a study of the site of the Medway raid support this statement? Explain your answer. You should refer to the site and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
Support for the statement (site evidence):
• Every layer of the site's defences failed through neglect: Sheerness unfinished, the chain's batteries unmanned, guardships skeleton-crewed, the fleet itself laid up unpaid.
• The scuttling of ships by the defenders and the desertion of pilots to the enemy show a system collapsing from within.
Against the statement (site evidence):
• Navigating great ships up a winding, shoal-banked, tidal river under fire was seamanship of the highest order, and De Ruyter's disciplined use of tides, fireships and boarding parties exploited each weakness precisely.
• The Dutch plan — seizing Sheerness first, forcing the chain, striking the moorings, withdrawing intact with a prize — shows judgement, not luck.
• Context: the raid was a calculated stroke to force better terms at Breda, timed for when England could not respond.
A developed judgement weighing neglect against skill, grounded in named site features, is required for the top level.

before.content_html:
A Cathedral as a Statement of Recovery

St Paul’s Cathedral is your specified site for the 2028 exam. The building you can visit is mostly later than 1685, so be clear about what the examiner wants: the Restoration story of the site — the old cathedral’s destruction in the Great Fire of 1666, the argument over what should replace it, Christopher Wren’s designs, and the start of construction in 1675, with the walls rising through the last decade of Charles II’s reign. Read that story and the site becomes a summary of Restoration England: disaster, recovery, the new science, and the alliance of Crown and Church.

Old St Paul's: A Ruin Before the Fire

The medieval cathedral on Ludgate Hill — the highest ground in the City — was one of the largest churches in Europe, and by 1660 one of the shabbiest. Its great spire had been destroyed by lightning in 1561 and never rebuilt; under the Commonwealth the nave had been used as cavalry stables; the fabric was cracked and patched. In August 1666 the young Christopher Wren — an Oxford astronomer turned architect — submitted a report proposing to crown the crumbling crossing with something England had never seen: a dome. Days later, the question became academic.

Key Fact

In the Great Fire of September 1666 (Lesson 6) the cathedral burned with the City around it. Booksellers had stacked their stock in the crypt for safety; it burned with everything else. Falling masonry and melted roof-lead left the great church an unstable shell, and after attempts at patching, demolition was accepted as unavoidable.

Wren and the Battle of the Designs

Rebuilding the cathedral of England’s capital was an argument about what England now was, and it ran for nearly a decade. Wren’s favourite scheme, preserved in the huge oak Great Model of 1673–4, was radical: a centralised church under a vast dome — classical, geometric, continental. The clergy rejected it; a cathedral, they insisted, needed the long nave and choir of English tradition. The compromise came in 1675: the so-called Warrant Design, a conventional long-plan church approved by royal warrant — to which Charles II added a quietly decisive clause, allowing Wren liberty to make ‘variations, rather ornamental than essential’ as the work proceeded. Wren used that licence to transform the approved design, and what rose from 1675 was far closer to his own vision, crowned in the end by the dome the clergy had refused on paper.

Wren was a founder of the Royal Society (Lesson 10) and a professor of astronomy before he was an architect, and his collaborator Robert Hooke — the Society’s great experimenter — helped survey the ruined City and design its rebuilding. St Paul’s is what the new science looked like in stone: structural problems attacked with geometry and experiment. The site ties Lesson 6 (the Fire) to Lesson 10 (the Royal Society) in a single building — a connection examiners reward.

Paying for It: The Coal Tax

A bankrupt-ish Crown (Lesson 13) could not simply buy a cathedral. The money came instead from the Rebuilding Acts’ coal tax — a duty on every ton of coal landed in London, the fuel of the city’s hearths and trades. It was a shrewd instrument: broad, steady, collected at the port, and paid in pennies by everyone who warmed themselves in the capital. London, in effect, rebuilt its own cathedral by heating itself. The same fund rebuilt dozens of Wren’s parish churches, whose steeples rose around St Paul’s in a single co-ordinated skyline — the most visible public-works programme of the age.

The Building Rises

The foundation stone was laid in June 1675, and by the end of Charles II’s reign in 1685 the choir walls stood well advanced — a working answer, in Portland stone, to anyone who doubted the City would recover. The cathedral took thirty-five years in all: the choir opened for the thanksgiving service for the Peace of Ryswick in December 1697, and Parliament declared the work complete in 1711, with Wren still alive to see it — a cathedral begun and finished under one architect, something no medieval builder ever managed. The dome, rising some 365 feet, made a new crown for London’s skyline on the site where the lightning-struck spire had once stood.

Key Fact

The coal tax under the Rebuilding Acts financed St Paul’s and the rebuilt City churches together — a co-ordinated skyline of Wren steeples around one dome, paid for by a duty on the fuel Londoners burned.

What the Site Shows About Restoration England

Each layer of the story is evidence. The decayed old cathedral shows the scars the Restoration inherited — Reformation, neglect and Civil War abuse written into the fabric. The Fire shows the fragility of the wooden city (Lesson 6). The design battle shows a nation negotiating between tradition and the new — clergy defending the English past, a scientist-architect importing classical Europe, a king umpiring with a clause. The coal tax shows practical, parliamentary finance doing what the royal purse could not. And the rising walls show confidence itself: a regime that had survived plague, fire and the Dutch in three consecutive years (Lessons 5, 6 and 13) declaring in Portland stone that London’s future would outshine its past.

Using the Site in the Exam

Chain features to meanings. Old St Paul’s stabled and spireless → the inheritance of civil war; the crypt of burned books → the Fire’s cost to trade and learning; the Great Model → the ambition of the new science; the clergy’s rejection and the Warrant → the pull of tradition; the ‘ornamental’ clause → how Charles II managed rivals; the coal tax → recovery financed by ordinary Londoners; the walls rising by 1685 → confidence restored within your period. Feature, meaning, link to the statement — and keep your evidence anchored in 1660–1685, using the later completion only as the outcome the period made possible.
before.exam_tip_html: Date discipline wins marks on this site. The finished dome belongs to 1710, outside your period — so build answers on what happened by 1685: the ruin, the demolition, the design battle of 1670–75, the coal tax, the foundation stone and the rising choir. Use the completed cathedral only as the destination the Restoration set course for, and the examiner sees a student in control of the chronology.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of Old St Paul's on the eve of the Great Fire.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• One of Europe's largest medieval churches, on Ludgate Hill, the highest ground in the City.
• Its spire had been destroyed by lightning in 1561 and never replaced.
• Decay and misuse: cracked, patched fabric, and a nave used as cavalry stables under the Commonwealth.
• Wren's August 1666 report proposing to crown the crossing with a dome — days before the Fire.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the design finally approved for the new St Paul's in 1675.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• The Warrant Design: a traditional long-plan cathedral with nave and choir, approved by royal warrant after the clergy rejected the domed Great Model.
• The royal clause permitting 'variations, rather ornamental than essential', which Wren used to transform the design during construction.
• Classical construction in Portland stone, replacing the Gothic of the old cathedral.
• Its funding framework — the coal tax under the Rebuilding Acts.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the argument over the design of the new St Paul's.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• It shows tradition against innovation: clergy defending the English long-plan cathedral against a scientist-architect's centralised classical dome.
• It shows how Charles II governed: rather than impose a side he approved the traditional design and quietly armed Wren with the variations clause.
• It shows the prestige of the new science: the Royal Society's geometry and experiment reshaping the nation's chief church.
• The outcome — a warrant on paper, a dome in the sky — shows where cultural authority was actually moving in Restoration England.

practice_questions.text: Write an account of what happened to St Paul's between 1666 and 1685.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• September 1666: the Great Fire guts the old cathedral; the booksellers' stock stored in the crypt burns; the shell proves unstable.
• Late 1660s: patching attempts fail and demolition is accepted; Wren emerges as the architect of the rebuilding.
• 1670-75: the design battle — First Model, the rejected Great Model of 1673-4, and the 1675 Warrant Design with the royal variations clause.
• 1675-85: the foundation stone laid in June 1675, coal-tax funding flowing, and the choir walls well advanced in Portland stone by the end of Charles II's reign.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the coal tax for the rebuilding of London's churches.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• It solved the central problem — a Crown that could not pay (the same poverty exposed on the Medway in 1667) — with a steady parliamentary duty collected at the port.
• It spread the cost in pennies across everyone who burned coal in London: the city rebuilt its own cathedral by heating itself.
• It funded a programme, not just a building: dozens of Wren parish churches rose with St Paul's as a co-ordinated new skyline.
• Its reliability made a thirty-five-year project financeable — long-term public works from long-term public revenue.

practice_questions.text: 'The rebuilding of St Paul's shows the confidence of Restoration England more than its problems.' How far does a study of St Paul's support this statement? Explain your answer. You should refer to St Paul's and your contextual knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
Support for the statement (site evidence):
• The decision itself: after plague, fire and the Medway humiliation in three years, England chose to build Europe's grandest new cathedral — recovery declared in Portland stone.
• The Royal Society connection: Wren and Hooke rebuilding with geometry and experiment shows a culture confident in its new science.
• Steady coal-tax finance and walls rising by 1685 show institutions capable of sustaining a generation-long project.
Against the statement (site evidence):
• The site records the problems first: a cathedral ruined by neglect, civil war stabling and fire — the Restoration inherited and suffered catastrophe before it built.
• The design battle shows a divided culture, and the Crown's inability to fund the work itself echoes the bankruptcy behind the Medway disaster.
• Completion lay far beyond the period — in 1685 confidence was a promissory note, not a finished dome.
A developed judgement weighing declared confidence against inherited fragility is required for the top level.
